title: Sequences & Series
description: Arithmetic and geometric sequences, series sums, sigma notation, and applications including compound interest.

notes.heading: Arithmetic Sequences and Series
notes.body:
An arithmetic sequence is a list of numbers where each term changes by a fixed amount.

📌 Definition
A sequence is arithmetic if the difference between consecutive terms is constant:
    $$d = u_{n+1} - u_n$$

🔑 Key Formulas
    nth term:     $$u_n = u_1 + (n - 1)d$$
    Sum of $n$ terms:
        $$S_n = \dfrac{n}{2} \left[2u_1 + (n - 1)d\right]$$
        or $$S_n = \dfrac{n}{2}(u_1 + u_n)$$

💡 Worked Example
The fourth term of an arithmetic sequence is 10 and the ninth term is 25. Find the first term and common difference.

  Step 1: Set up two equations
    $$u_4 = u_1 + 3d = 10$$
    $$u_9 = u_1 + 8d = 25$$

  Step 2: Subtract the first equation from the second
    $$5d = 15$$
    $$d = 3$$

  Step 3: Substitute back to find $u_1$
    $$u_1 + 3(3) = 10$$
    $$u_1 = 1$$

  Answer: $u_1 = 1$, $d = 3$

💡 Worked Example
Find the sum of the first 20 terms of the sequence 3, 7, 11, 15, ...

  Step 1: Identify $u_1$ and $d$
    $$u_1 = 3, \quad d = 7 - 3 = 4$$

  Step 2: Use the sum formula
    $$S_{20} = \dfrac{20}{2} 	imes \left[2(3) + (20 - 1)(4)\right]$$
    $$S_{20} = 10 	imes (6 + 76)$$
    $$S_{20} = 10 	imes 82$$
    $$S_{20} = 820$$

📎 Key Points to Remember
• Simple interest and straight-line depreciation both follow arithmetic patterns
• The formula $S_n = \dfrac{n}{2}(u_1 + u_n)$ is fastest when you know the first and last terms
• Use $S_n = \dfrac{n}{2}\left[2u_1 + (n - 1)d\right]$ when you know the common difference instead

⚠️ Common Mistake
Forgetting that the nth term formula uses $(n - 1)$, not $n$. The first term already exists — you only add the common difference $(n - 1)$ times.

illustration.alt: Arithmetic sequences with common difference d and nth term uₙ=u₁+(n−1)d; geometric sequences with common ratio r and nth term uₙ=u₁rⁿ⁻¹; sum formulas for both; and the infinite geometric series sum S∞=u₁/(1−r) when |r|<1.
illustration.caption: Arithmetic sequences have a constant difference; geometric sequences have a constant ratio. The sum formulas let you add terms efficiently. Infinite geometric series converge when |r|<1.

notes.heading: Geometric Sequences and Series
notes.body:
A geometric sequence is a list of numbers where each term is multiplied by a fixed amount to get the next.

📌 Definition
A sequence is geometric if the ratio between consecutive terms is constant:
    $$r = \dfrac{u_{n+1}}{u_n}$$

🔑 Key Formulas
    nth term:     $$u_n = u_1 	imes r^{n - 1}$$
    Sum of $n$ terms ($r 
eq 1$):
        $$S_n = \dfrac{u_1(r^n - 1)}{r - 1}$$
        or $$S_n = \dfrac{u_1(1 - r^n)}{1 - r}$$

💡 Worked Example
The sixth term of a geometric sequence is 486 and the seventh term is 1458. Find the common ratio and first term.

  Step 1: Find the common ratio
    $$r = \dfrac{u_7}{u_6} = \dfrac{1458}{486} = 3$$

  Step 2: Use the nth term formula to find $u_1$
    $$u_6 = u_1 	imes 3^5 = 486$$
    $$u_1 	imes 243 = 486$$
    $$u_1 = 2$$

  Answer: $r = 3$, $u_1 = 2$

💡 Worked Example
A geometric sequence has $u_1 = 25$ and $r = 0.8$. Find $u_5$ and $S_5$.

  Step 1: Find the fifth term
    $$u_5 = 25 	imes (0.8)^4$$
    $$u_5 = 25 	imes 0.4096$$
    $$u_5 = 10.24$$

  Step 2: Find the sum of five terms
    $$S_5 = \dfrac{25 	imes (1 - 0.8^5)}{1 - 0.8}$$
    $$S_5 = \dfrac{25 	imes (1 - 0.32768)}{0.2}$$
    $$S_5 = 25 	imes 3.3616$$
    $$S_5 = 84.04$$

📎 Real-World Applications
• Compound interest: $FV = PV 	imes (1 + r)^n$
• Population growth and radioactive decay
• Spread of bacteria and viruses

⚠️ Common Mistake
Using the wrong sum formula. When $r > 1$, use $S_n = \dfrac{u_1(r^n - 1)}{r - 1}$. When $0 < r < 1$, use $S_n = \dfrac{u_1(1 - r^n)}{1 - r}$ to avoid negative denominators.

notes.heading: Sum to Infinity
notes.body:
Some geometric series keep adding up forever — yet they still settle on a single number.

📌 Definition
A geometric series converges when the terms get closer and closer to zero. This happens only when the common ratio is between $-1$ and $1$.

🔑 Formula
    If $|r| < 1$:     $$S_\infty = \dfrac{u_1}{1 - r}$$
    If $|r| \geq 1$:     The series diverges (no finite sum)

💡 Worked Example
The first three terms of a geometric sequence are 6, 2, and $\dfrac{2}{3}$. Explain why the series converges and find the sum to infinity.

  Step 1: Find the common ratio
    $$r = \dfrac{2}{6} = \dfrac{1}{3}$$

  Step 2: Check convergence
    $$\left|\dfrac{1}{3}\right| = \dfrac{1}{3} < 1$$
    The series converges because $|r| < 1$.

  Step 3: Calculate $S_\infty$
    $$S_\infty = \dfrac{6}{1 - \dfrac{1}{3}}$$
    $$S_\infty = \dfrac{6}{\dfrac{2}{3}}$$
    $$S_\infty = 6 	imes \dfrac{3}{2}$$
    $$S_\infty = 9$$

💡 Worked Example
Does the series $1 + \dfrac{1}{2} + \dfrac{1}{4} + \dfrac{1}{8} + \ldots$ have a finite sum?

  Step 1: Identify $u_1$ and $r$
    $$u_1 = 1, \quad r = \dfrac{1}{2}$$

  Step 2: Check $|r|$
    $$\left|\dfrac{1}{2}\right| < 1$$ → converges

  Step 3: Calculate $S_\infty$
    $$S_\infty = \dfrac{1}{1 - \dfrac{1}{2}} = \dfrac{1}{\dfrac{1}{2}} = 2$$

📎 Key Points to Remember
• Always verify $|r| < 1$ before applying the $S_\infty$ formula
• The sum to infinity is a limit — the partial sums get closer and closer but never exceed it
• Alternating sequences with negative $r$ can still converge if $|r| < 1$

⚠️ Common Mistake
Applying $S_\infty = \dfrac{u_1}{1 - r}$ without checking $|r|$ first. If $r = 2$, the formula gives a negative number, which is clearly wrong because the terms are all positive and growing.

notes.heading: Sigma Notation
notes.body:
Sigma notation is a compact way to write the sum of many terms in a sequence.

📌 Definition
The Greek letter $sum$ (sigma) means "sum." The expression to the right tells you what to add, and the limits above and below tell you where to start and stop.

    $$\sum_{k=m}^{n} u_k = u_m + u_{m+1} + \ldots + u_n$$

🔑 Key Properties
    $$\sum_{k=1}^{n} \left[u_k + v_k\right] = \sum_{k=1}^{n} u_k + \sum_{k=1}^{n} v_k$$
    $$\sum_{k=1}^{n} c \cdot u_k = c \cdot \sum_{k=1}^{n} u_k$$

💡 Worked Example
Write $u_1 + u_2 + u_3 + \ldots + u_6$ in sigma notation, given $u_n = 2 	imes 3^{n-1}$.

  Step 1: Identify the pattern
    Each term has the form $2 	imes 3^{n-1}$

  Step 2: Write in sigma notation
    $$\sum_{n=1}^{6} 2 	imes 3^{n-1}$$

💡 Worked Example
Evaluate $\sum_{k=3}^{7} (2k + 1)$.

  Step 1: Recognise the lower limit is not 1
    Rewrite as $\sum_{k=1}^{7} (2k + 1) - \sum_{k=1}^{2} (2k + 1)$

  Step 2: Evaluate each sum
    $$\sum_{k=1}^{7}: 3 + 5 + 7 + 9 + 11 + 13 + 15 = 63$$
    $$\sum_{k=1}^{2}: 3 + 5 = 8$$

  Step 3: Subtract
    $$63 - 8 = 55$$

📎 Key Points to Remember
• The variable below $sum$ is the index (commonly $k$, $i$, or $n$)
• Always check whether the lower limit starts at 1 or another number
• Identify whether the underlying sequence is arithmetic or geometric before applying a sum formula

⚠️ Common Mistake
Changing the limits incorrectly when rewriting a sigma expression. If you shift the index, you must adjust the limits AND the formula inside.

notes.heading: Depreciation, Simple Interest & Compounding Periods
notes.body:
Financial mathematics uses sequences and series to model how money grows or shrinks over time.

📌 Simple Interest
Interest is paid only on the original principal. This creates an arithmetic sequence.

    $$FV = PV 	imes (1 + rt)$$

    $PV$ = present value (principal)
    $r$ = annual interest rate (as a decimal)
    $t$ = time in years

📌 Compound Interest
Interest is paid on the principal AND on previously earned interest. This creates a geometric sequence.

    $$FV = PV 	imes \left(1 + \dfrac{r}{100k}\right)^{kn}$$

    $PV$ = present value
    $r$ = nominal annual interest rate ($\%$)
    $k$ = compounding periods per year
    $n$ = number of years

🔑 Common Values of $k$
• Annually:      $k = 1$
• Half-yearly:   $k = 2$
• Quarterly:     $k = 4$
• Monthly:       $k = 12$

📌 Depreciation
Value decreases by a fixed percentage each year. This is compound interest with subtraction.

    $$FV = PV 	imes \left(1 - \dfrac{r}{100}\right)^n$$

💡 Worked Example
Kim invests MYR 2000 at a nominal annual rate of $2.5\%$ compounded monthly. Find the value after 5 years.

  Step 1: Identify the values
    $$PV = 2000, \quad r = 2.5, \quad k = 12, \quad n = 5$$

  Step 2: Substitute into the formula
    $$FV = 2000 	imes \left(1 + \dfrac{2.5}{100 	imes 12}\right)^{12 	imes 5}$$
    $$FV = 2000 	imes (1 + 0.002083\ldots)^{60}$$
    $$FV = 2000 	imes 1.133148\ldots$$
    $$FV \approx 2266.30$$

  Answer: MYR 2266.30

💡 Worked Example
A new laptop costs \$1200 and depreciates by $20\%$ each year. What is its value after 3 years?

  Step 1: Use the depreciation formula
    $$FV = 1200 	imes \left(1 - \dfrac{20}{100}\right)^3$$
    $$FV = 1200 	imes (0.8)^3$$
    $$FV = 1200 	imes 0.512$$
    $$FV = 614.40$$

  Answer: \$614.40

📎 Key Points to Remember
• Simple interest forms an arithmetic sequence (constant difference)
• Compound interest and depreciation form geometric sequences (constant ratio)
• More compounding periods per year means more interest earned

⚠️ Common Mistake
Using $r/k$ directly as a decimal without dividing by 100 first. The formula uses $r$ as a percentage, so $5\%$ becomes $\dfrac{5}{100k}$, not $\dfrac{5}{k}$.

notes.heading: Recurrence Relations
notes.body:
An explicit formula gives $u_n$ directly from $n$. A recurrence relation builds each term from earlier terms.

📌 Definition
A recurrence relation defines each term of a sequence using one or more earlier terms, together with a starting value.
    $$u_{n+1} = f(u_n), \quad u_1 = a$$
For arithmetic sequences this becomes $u_{n+1} = u_n + d$.
For geometric sequences this becomes $u_{n+1} = u_n 	imes r$.

🔑 Key Concept
To generate terms, repeatedly apply the rule using the previous term. To find an explicit formula, solve the recurrence.

💡 Worked Example
A sequence is defined by $u_{n+1} = 2u_n + 1$ with $u_1 = 3$. Find the first five terms.

  Step 1: Apply the rule repeatedly
    $$u_2 = 2(3) + 1 = 7$$
    $$u_3 = 2(7) + 1 = 15$$
    $$u_4 = 2(15) + 1 = 31$$
    $$u_5 = 2(31) + 1 = 63$$

  Answer: $3, 7, 15, 31, 63$

📎 Key Points to Remember
• Arithmetic and geometric sequences are special cases of recurrence relations
• A recurrence needs a starting value; without it the sequence is not fully defined
• Some recurrence relations cannot be solved with the standard arithmetic or geometric formulas

⚠️ Common Mistake
Confusing the index. In $u_{n+1} = u_n + d$, the common difference is added once per step, so $u_n = u_1 + (n-1)d$, not $u_1 + nd$.

notes.heading: Identifying Arithmetic and Geometric Sequences
notes.body:
Before using a formula, decide whether a sequence is arithmetic, geometric, or neither.

📌 Definition
• A sequence is arithmetic if the difference between consecutive terms is constant: $d = u_{n+1} - u_n$
• A sequence is geometric if the ratio between consecutive terms is constant: $r = \dfrac{u_{n+1}}{u_n}$

🔑 How it works
First check the differences between consecutive terms. If they are equal, the sequence is arithmetic. If they change, check the ratios. Equal ratios mean the sequence is geometric.

💡 Worked Example
Identify the type of sequence $5, 9, 13, 17, \ldots$

  Step 1: Check the differences
    $$9 - 5 = 4, \quad 13 - 9 = 4, \quad 17 - 13 = 4$$

  The differences are constant, so the sequence is arithmetic with $d = 4$.

💡 Worked Example
Identify the type of sequence $2, 6, 18, 54, \ldots$

  Step 1: Check the ratios
    $$\dfrac{6}{2} = 3, \quad \dfrac{18}{6} = 3, \quad \dfrac{54}{18} = 3$$

  The ratios are constant, so the sequence is geometric with $r = 3$.

📎 Key Points to Remember
• A sequence can be neither arithmetic nor geometric
• Terms that alternate in sign often indicate a negative common ratio
• Financial contexts: simple interest follows an arithmetic pattern; compound interest and depreciation follow geometric patterns

⚠️ Common Mistake
Using geometric formulas on an arithmetic sequence. Always test for a common difference first.

notes.heading: Harder Exam-Style Applications
notes.body:
This note brings together sigma notation, geometric series word problems, compound interest series, recurrence relations, and convergence in harder exam-style questions.

🔑 Sigma Notation for a Geometric Series

💡 Worked Example
Write the infinite geometric series $8+4+2+1+\ldots$ using sigma notation and find its sum.

  Step 1: Identify $u_1$ and $r$
    $$u_1=8, \quad r=\dfrac{1}{2}$$

  Step 2: Write the nth term
    $$u_n = 8 	imes \left(\dfrac{1}{2}\right)^{n-1}$$

  Step 3: Write the series in sigma notation
    $$\sum_{n=1}^{\infty} 8 	imes \left(\dfrac{1}{2}\right)^{n-1}$$

  Step 4: Check convergence and sum
    $$|r|=\dfrac{1}{2}<1 \quad \Rightarrow \quad S_\infty = \dfrac{8}{1-\dfrac{1}{2}} = 16$$

🔑 Geometric Series Word Problem

💡 Worked Example
A ball is dropped from 10 m and rebounds to 60% of its previous height. Find the total distance travelled before it comes to rest.

  Step 1: Downward distance
    First drop = 10 m

  Step 2: Up and down after the first bounce
    Each rebound is 0.6 of the previous height, so the combined up-and-down distances form an infinite geometric series:
    $$2	imes10	imes0.6 + 2	imes10	imes0.6^2 + \ldots$$

  Step 3: Sum the rebounds
    $$2	imes10	imes0.6 	imes \dfrac{1}{1-0.6} = 12 	imes \dfrac{1}{0.4} = 30$$

  Step 4: Add the original drop
    $$10 + 30 = 40 	ext{ m}$$

🔑 Compound Interest as a Series

💡 Worked Example
Tom deposits \$100 at the start of each year into an account paying 4% per annum. Find the value immediately after the third deposit.

  Step 1: Each deposit earns compound interest for a different number of years
    First deposit: \$100 $	imes 1.04^3$
    Second deposit: \$100 $	imes 1.04^2$
    Third deposit: \$100 $	imes 1.04^1$

  Step 2: Write as a geometric series
    $$FV = 100(1.04) + 100(1.04)^2 + 100(1.04)^3$$
    First term $a=100	imes1.04$, common ratio $r=1.04$, $n=3$

  Step 3: Apply the sum formula
    $$FV = \dfrac{100	imes1.04\left(1.04^3 - 1\right)}{1.04 - 1}$$
    $$FV \approx \$324.65$$

🔑 From Recurrence Relation to Explicit Formula

💡 Worked Example
A sequence is defined by $u_{n+1}=3u_n-4$ with $u_1=2$. Find an explicit formula for $u_n$.

  Step 1: Find the fixed point $L$
    At equilibrium $L=3L-4$, so $L=2$

  Step 2: Define a new sequence $v_n = u_n - L$
    Then $v_{n+1}=u_{n+1}-2=3u_n-4-2=3(u_n-2)=3v_n$
    So $v_n$ is geometric with $v_1=u_1-2=0$

  Step 3: Conclude
    Since $v_1=0$, every $v_n=0$, so $u_n=2$ for all $n$.

  Answer: $u_n=2$

🔑 Convergence with an Unknown Common Ratio

💡 Worked Example
The infinite geometric series $a+ar+ar^2+\ldots$ has first term 5 and sum 20. Find $r$.

  Step 1: Use the sum-to-infinity formula
    $$S_\infty = \dfrac{a}{1-r} = 20$$

  Step 2: Substitute $a=5$
    $$\dfrac{5}{1-r}=20$$
    $$1-r = \dfrac{5}{20} = \dfrac{1}{4}$$
    $$r = \dfrac{3}{4}$$

  Step 3: Check convergence
    $$|r|=\dfrac{3}{4}<1$$, so the series converges.

📎 Key Points to Remember
• Sigma notation can describe both finite and infinite series
• Geometric series model repeated percentage change, including bouncing balls and regular deposits
• A recurrence relation can often be converted to an explicit formula by finding a fixed point
• Always check $|r|<1$ before using $S_\infty = \dfrac{u_1}{1-r}$

⚠️ Common Mistake
Forgetting the first drop in a bouncing-ball problem. The initial fall is not doubled, but every rebound has both an upward and a downward part.

flashcards.definition: Interest paid only on the original principal; forms an arithmetic sequence.
Value decreases by a fixed percentage each year: $FV = PV \cdot \left(1 - \dfrac{r}{100}\right)^n$.
When $r < 0$, terms alternate positive and negative.
A rule that defines each term using previous term(s), e.g. $u_{n+1}=u_n+d$ or $u_{n+1}=r\,u_n$.
Compact notation for a sum: $\sum_{k=m}^{n} u_k = u_m+u_{m+1}+\ldots+u_n$.

questions.stem: Arithmetic: $u_4=18$, $u_7=30$. Common difference?
questions.explanation: $3d = 30-18 = 12$ \rightarrow $d = 4$.

questions.stem: Sum of first 20 terms of $3+7+11+\ldots$?
questions.explanation: This is an arithmetic series with first term $u_1=3$ and common difference $d=4$. The 20th term is $u_{20}=3+(20-1)(4)=79$. The sum of the first $n$ terms is $S_n=\dfrac{n}{2}(u_1+u_n)$, so $S_{20}=\dfrac{20}{2}(3+79)=10\times82=820$. This formula is used to total regular savings or distances.

questions.stem: Convergent: $u_1=12$, $r=\dfrac{1}{4}$. $S_\infty?$
\$5000 at $4\%$ compound interest for 3 years?
A student invests £2000 at a nominal annual rate of $3.6\%$ compounded monthly. What is the value after 5 years?
questions.explanation: $FV = 2000\cdot(1+0.003)^{60} \approx 2000\cdot1.197$ £2394. Monthly compounding beats annual (£2387) and simple interest (£2360).

questions.stem: A new laptop costs \$1200 and depreciates by $20\%$ each year. What is its value after 3 years?
questions.explanation: $FV = 1200\cdot(0.8)^3 = 1200\cdot0.512 = 614.40$ \$614.40. \$600 is linear depreciation (wrong model), \$768 is after only 2 years.

questions.stem: Which of the following geometric sequences does NOT have a finite sum to infinity?
questions.explanation: $S_\infty$ exists only when $|r|<1$. Here $|-1.2|=1.2 \geq 1$, so the series diverges. The others all have $|r|<1$.

questions.stem: A geometric sequence has $u_1=2$ and $r=-3$. What is $u_6?$
questions.explanation: $u_6 = 2\cdot(-3)^5 = 2\cdot(-243) = -486$. The negative ratio makes terms alternate; odd powers of $r$ are negative.

questions.stem: A geometric sequence has $u_1=4$ and $r=1.5$. Which term is the first to exceed 100?
questions.explanation: Solve $4\cdot1.5^{n-1} > 100$. Taking logs: $n-1 > \dfrac{\ln 25}{\ln 1.5} \approx 7.94$, so $n > 8.94$. The 9th term ($\approx 102.5$) is first to exceed 100.

questions.stem: Ali invests \$2000 for 4 years at $5\%$ per year. How much more would he earn with compound interest (compounded annually) than with simple interest?
questions.explanation: Simple interest: $2000 + 4	imes100 = 2400$ \$2400. Compound: $2000	imes1.05^4 \approx 2431$ \$2431. The difference is about \$31. Compound interest earns "interest on interest," so it outperforms simple interest over time.

questions.stem: Evaluate $\sum_{k=1}^{4} (2k+1)$.
questions.explanation: Substitute $k=1,2,3,4$ into $2k+1$ and add: $3+5+7+9=24$.

questions.stem: A sequence is defined by $u_{n+1}=3u_n-2$ with $u_1=2$. Find $u_4$.
Which of the following sequences is geometric?
questions.explanation: $3,6,12,24$ has common ratio $r=2$. The other choices are arithmetic or neither.

questions.stem: For what value of $x$ does the geometric series $12+12x+12x^2+\ldots$ converge to $18$?
questions.explanation: $S_\infty=\dfrac{12}{1-x}=18$, so $1-x=\dfrac{2}{3}$ and $x=\dfrac{1}{3}$.

questions.stem: Evaluate $\sum_{k=1}^{10}\left(3\cdot2^k-4k\right)$.
questions.explanation: Split the sum. The arithmetic part is $\sum_{k=1}^{10}4k=4	imes55=220$. The geometric part is $\sum_{k=1}^{10}3\cdot2^k=3	imes(2^{11}-2)=6138$. Subtracting gives $6138-220=5918$.

questions.stem: A ball is dropped from 12 m and rebounds to 75% of its previous height. Find the total distance travelled before it comes to rest.
questions.explanation: After the first drop, every rebound has an upward and a downward part. The rebound distances form $2	imes12	imes0.75+2	imes12	imes0.75^2+\ldots$. Sum this infinite geometric series: $2	imes12	imes0.75\div(1-0.75)=72$. Add the original 12 m drop: $12+72=84$ m.

questions.stem: At the start of each month Eva deposits \$200 into an account that pays 0.5% interest per month. What is the account value immediately after the 12th deposit?
A sequence is defined by $u_{n+1}=p\,u_n+q$. Given $u_1=5$, $u_2=11$ and $u_3=23$, find $u_5$.
questions.explanation: From the recurrence, $5p+q=11$ and $11p+q=23$. Subtracting gives $6p=12$, so $p=2$ and $q=1$. Then $u_4=2(23)+1=47$ and $u_5=2(47)+1=95$.

questions.stem: For which values of $x$ does the geometric series $\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}(2x-1)^n$ converge?
questions.explanation: A geometric series converges when $|r|<1$. Here $r=2x-1$, so $|2x-1|<1$. Solving gives $-1<2x-1<1$, which simplifies to $0<x<1$.
